Plan this as a Rhylthyme recipe and deliver a live timeline: Sheet-Pan Chicken with Potatoes and Broccoli for 4 people
Resource limits: one oven, two sheet pans, one burner, one cook.

Source text (read all of it):
<<<
Sheet-Pan Chicken with Potatoes and Broccoli

A Tuesday dinner for four. One oven, two sheet pans, one burner, one cook. The potatoes need longer than the chicken and the broccoli needs least of all, so the two pans go in at different times and come out together.

Oven
Heat the oven to 425°F; 15 minutes. While it heats, toss the halved potatoes with oil and salt on the first sheet pan; 8 minutes. Slide the potatoes in and roast them for 15 minutes on their own.

Pat the chicken thighs dry, rub them with the spice mix and lay them on the second pan; 10 minutes. Put the second pan in when the potatoes have had their 15 minutes. Twenty minutes after the chicken goes in, pull both pans out, rotate them, tip the broccoli onto the potato pan and put everything back; 4 minutes. Roast for a final 15 minutes, until the thighs read 175°F and the broccoli is charred at the edges. Rest the chicken on a board for 8 minutes before slicing.

Pan sauce
Once the pans are out, tip the pan juices into a small pan, add stock and mustard and reduce for 6 minutes. Whisk in cold butter off the heat; 2 minutes. Keep the sauce off the flame until you plate.

Salad
Start the salad when the chicken goes in the oven, not before, or the leaves will sit around. Wash and dry the leaves; 6 minutes. Shake the vinaigrette together in a jar; 3 minutes. Dress the salad only when the chicken has been resting five minutes; 2 minutes.

Serve
Slice the thighs and plate everything; 6 minutes. Sauce goes over the chicken at the table.
>>>

Target data model, in my own words:

A track is one sequential line of work, so steps on the same track never overlap and genuinely concurrent activities, such as oven heating and pan preparation, belong in separate tracks. A step has exactly one duration kind: fixed with seconds, variable with minSeconds, maxSeconds, and defaultSeconds, or indefinite until the person stops it. A startTrigger places a step on the clock or links it to another step using programStart, programStartOffset, afterStep, afterStepWithBuffer, manual, onAbort, or compound. stepIds are unique across the whole program, not just within one track, because later steps reference them globally. Every task occupied by a step needs a matching resourceConstraints entry, and that entry’s maxConcurrent is what prevents two steps from sharing one oven, one burner, one sheet pan pool, or one work station at the same time. Repeated work is expressed with replicates on one step, chained by instances “each”, barriered by instances “all” where needed, and limited by maxInFlight when only k intermediate items can be held; this recipe does not obviously require replicates because the two pans have different work.

Expected resource constraints:

- oven: maxConcurrent 1 — all heating and roasting operations share the one oven.
- sheet_pan: maxConcurrent 2 — the recipe uses exactly two pans, one primarily for potatoes and one for chicken, with broccoli later moving onto the potato pan.
- burner: maxConcurrent 1 — the pan-sauce reduction needs the single burner; the butter is whisked in off heat.
- prep: maxConcurrent 1 — all active hands-on work is done by the one cook: potato toss, chicken drying and spicing, pulling/rotating pans, adding broccoli, sauce starting and finishing, salad work, slicing, and plating.
- rest_area: maxConcurrent 1 — if the 8-minute chicken rest is modeled as a visible step, it should occupy a passive resting space rather than the cook’s active prep capacity.
